Minsk Mazowiecki New Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Mińsk Mazowiecki, Poland

Not demolished. Jewish settlement in Mińsk Mazowiecki developed from the early 19th century, and the town became seat of the Novominsk Hasidic dynasty; by 1921, 4,130 Jews made up nearly 40% of the population, most murdered at Treblinka in 1942. Local synagogue leadership initiated this cemetery in 1873, finalizing the land purchase in 1878. In 1902, Rebbe Jakow Perłow, founder of the Nowy Mińsk Hasidic dynasty, was buried here. During WWII, Germans executed 218 people at the cemetery in December 1942 and buried participants of a school-camp uprising there in January 1943. Poland formally closed the cemetery in 1964; a road extension cut through part of the grounds in 1978. The Mińsk Jewish community in France funded a Holocaust memorial in 1965, and the Warsaw Jewish Religious Community, with European Jewish Cemeteries Initiative support, built a new fence in 2016-2017. About 500 tombstones survive, the oldest dated 1878; unmarked wartime mass graves are still visible as depressions in the ground.
